LETTER TO THE EDITORS
Ophthalmoplegia heralding the onset of anti-amphiphysin related
paraneoplastic stiff person syndrome
Maruthi R. Vinjam 1 • Priya Shanmugarajah 1 • Helen L. Ford 1
/C211Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg 2016
Dear Sirs,
A 47-year-old woman presented to her doctor with an
8-week history of generalised lethargy and weight loss. She
was found to have enlarged left axillary lymph nodes. She
went on to have an ultrasound guided biopsy which con-
���rmed grade 2 invasive ductal adenocarcinoma of left
breast. She had a wide local excision and axillary node
clearance followed by treatment with goserelin (hormone
treatment).
She presented to hospital 4 weeks later with persistent
neck pain, dizziness and episodes of unsteadiness. Cranial
nerve examination revealed ophthalmoplegia with restric-
ted horizontal pursuit and saccadic eye movements, with
intact vertical eye movements. There was no nystagmus or
diplopia as she was compensating this with head movement
similar to that seen in occulomotor apraxia. She had normal
motor, sensory examination of the limbs along with normal
cerebellar examination. She was investigated for possible
neoplastic and paraneoplastic phenomena in view of her
recent diagnosis of breast carcinoma. Her full blood count,
renal, septic screen, vasculitis screen and liver function
tests were normal. Her serum was tested for paraneoplastic
antibody screen (anti-Ma, anti-Yo, anti-Hu and anti-am-
phiphysin), acetylcholine receptor antibodies, anti-glycine
receptor, anti- gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), anti-
GQ1b and anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-Gad)
receptor antibodies. Two weeks into her admission, she
developed severe intermittent painful spasms triggered by
walking and emotions. Neuroimaging with MRI head and
spine with contrast, CSF analysis including cytology were
normal.
She progressively developed generalised stiffness with
severe axial and limb rigidity, which was exacerbated by
touch and emotions. Nerve co nduction studies and nee-
dle EMG done during ���rst we ek of hospital admission
were normal. All her blood tests were normal except for
her anti-amphiphysin antibodies which were positive
con���rming the diagnosis of s tiff person syndrome (SPS).
She later developed severe back spasms with opistho-
tonos and extensor spasms of both legs. She was unable
to walk. These symptoms partially responded to treat-
ment with benzodiazepines and oral baclofen. She had
persistent ophtha lmoplegia as described above. In the
next 2 weeks she developed type 2 respiratory failure
and dysphagia. She required non-invasive ventilation and
nasogastric feeding. She continued to deteriorate with
progressive dysphagia, restricted eye movement and
painful spasms.
She was treated with a 5-day course of intravenous
immunoglobulins, followed by ���ve cycles of plasma
exchange which resulted in only partial resolution of the
stiffness. She was then commenced on six cycles of adju-
vent chemotherapy with epirubicin and cyclophosphamide
with pegylated G-CSF cover. This resulted in signi���cant
improvement in her symptoms. She was weaned from
ventilator support and the dysphagia, painful stiffness and
rigidity resolved gradually. The restricted eye movements
signi���cantly improved, but not completely resolved at the
time of hospital discharge. She was commenced on adju-
ant endocrine therapy with fulvestrant injections. She was
transferred to a neuro-rehabilitation unit for further reha-
bilitation after a total inpatient admission of 8 months.
Franco et al. [ 1] ���rst described auto-antibodies directed
against a 128-kDa brain protein in breast cancer patients
& Maruthi R. Vinjam
1 Department of Neurology, Leeds Centre for Neurosciences,
Leeds General In���rmary, Leeds LS1 3EX, UK

DOI 10.1007/s00415-016-8078-3

presenting with stiff person syndrome (SPS). We report a
case of an anti-amphiphysin antibody related eye move-
ment disorder heralding the onset of SPS. Classical SPS
presents with severe stiffness, spasms triggered by touch
and emotions and is commonly associated with elevated
Anti-GAD antibodies. Anti-amphiphysin antibody associ-
ated SPS is thought to be distinctive syndrome with slightly
different clinical features [ 2] with a strong association to
breast cancer. These antibodies are thought to be patho-
genic as stiff person like syndrome was noted in rats with
intrathecal anti-amphiphysin antibody transfer [ 3]. Oph-
halmoplegia, oscillopsia and nystagmus have been
described in anti-GAD related SPS [ 4]. This is thought to
be due to GABA depletion. Our case has similarities to
patients described in anti-glycine receptor antibody related
progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
(PERM) [5]. Our patient had prolonged inpatient admission
and her stiffness only resolved after starting aggressive
chemotherapy for the underlying carcinoma. There was
only a partial response to treatment with immunoglobulins
and plasma exchange. Patients with SPS are likely to have
low performance status scoring on conventional perfor-
mance scales like the Karnofsky Performance Scale Index
which is used as a predictor for treatment outcomes by
oncologist. We recommend aggressive treatment of the
underlying cancer in this dif���cult patient group despite low
Karnofsky scores.
